items.s: Many shops now sell food in paper ____ instead of plastic.

giving a false impression of something

items.s: You are ____ in a supermarket with two bottles of shampoo.
When a company ____ a product seem better than it is, this is greenwashing.

tfn.s: The airlines were told not to use those claims in the same way again.
tfn.why: The text says: "The airlines were told not to use those claims in the same way again."

tfn.s: The label on the shampoo bottle explains what has improved.
tfn.why: The text says: "the label never explains what has actually improved".

tfn.s: The airlines had to pay a fine.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not mention any fine.

tfn.s: Every company that uses green advertising is dishonest.
tfn.why: The text says: "Not every business using green advertising is dishonest".

tfn.s: The writer says small improvements are worth making.
tfn.why: The text says: "small improvements are worth making".

pre.d: making a product sound better for nature than it really is
a piece of paper on a product with information about it
made again from old things, like old plastic
an official group that checks companies follow the rules
to do something good to make up for something bad
gases that go into the air from cars, planes and factories
something that shows clearly that a thing is true
a statement that says something is true

focus.note: Linking words join ideas. Use but and although for a difference, because for a reason and so for a result.

items.s: The label used green leaves, ____ it did not say what had improved.
The airlines were criticised ____ their adverts gave a misleading impression.
The shop sells cheap soap. ____, it is not made from recycled plastic.

A flashy slogan can ____ shoppers from the real cost of a product.

match.d: provide evidence that supports a claim
not to be trusted or depended on
succeed in the end against competition

items.s: By the time she reached the till, the shopper ____ to buy the greener bottle.
Claims that cannot be proved ____ under the new rules.
At the moment the message arrived, the shopper ____ two bottles.
In July 2026, Britain's regulator ____ complaints about two airlines.

tfn.s: The regulator decided that Eurowings and Qatar Airways had provided enough evidence for their claims.
tfn.why: The text says: "the companies had not provided enough evidence to support that impression".

tfn.s: An advertisement can seem green because of one detail, even if the rest of the business has barely changed.
tfn.why: The text says: "A single green detail can carry a whole advertisement, even when the rest of the business has barely changed."

tfn.s: Most airlines have stopped using offsetting claims since July 2026.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not say what airlines in general have done.

tfn.s: A product that uses less plastic always has a lower overall environmental impact.
tfn.why: The text says a product "may use less plastic but require more energy to make".

tfn.s: The new European Union rules also cover unreliable sustainability labels.
tfn.why: The text says: "The legislation also addresses unreliable sustainability labels".

pre.d: the idea or feeling you get about something
gases released into the air by vehicles, factories and planes
an official body that makes sure companies follow the rules
statements that you are not happy about something
laws made by a government
balancing harm by paying for something good elsewhere
able to continue without damaging the environment
choosing only some things and ignoring others

focus.note: Check the logic. Whereas shows a contrast between two things, provided adds a condition, and despite needs a noun or an -ing form.

items.s: ____ being technically accurate, the advert left a false impression.
Some shoppers read every label, ____ others simply trust the packaging.
Customers cannot check every claim; ____, independent checks are important.
A product may use less plastic. ____, it may need more energy to make.

Any company making bold environmental promises should expect close ____ from journalists and regulators.
The portrait of the factory was so ____ that it ignored its pollution record entirely.
Paying for a tree to be planted is not ____ to cutting your own emissions.

Emissions at the plant have fallen ____ since the new system was installed, though not to zero.

match.d: use something easier when nothing better works
avoid dealing with an awkward fact

items.s: The company's refusal to publish data raised doubts about the ____ of its claims.
Critics described the slogan as ____, since it implied a benefit that did not exist.

Offsetting schemes are often criticised for their lack of ____.

tfn.s: A company could be criticised for an advert in which every individual statement is true.
tfn.why: The text says each statement can be true while "the overall impression remains flattering, selective and misleading".

tfn.s: The writer believes offsetting schemes never fund useful work.
tfn.why: The text says: "An offset scheme may fund useful work".

tfn.s: The airlines appealed against the rulings of the Advertising Standards Authority.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not say how the airlines responded.

tfn.s: The writer argues that simplifying environmental information is dishonest in every case.
tfn.why: The text says: "Simplification is not dishonest in itself".

tfn.s: Judging a product only by the emissions from making it could give a misleading picture.
tfn.why: The text says a reusable product may have "a higher manufacturing footprint but a lower impact over time".

pre.d: soft and not bright
uses something unfairly for your own benefit
able to be supported with good reasons
balancing out damage by paying for good work elsewhere
situations where you give up one good thing to get another
new plans or actions to solve a problem
strong statements that something is true
decided that a complaint was right

focus.note: These are formal. Albeit introduces a contrast, hence gives a result after a semicolon, and notwithstanding is followed by a noun.

items.s: The advert was accurate in its wording, ____ misleading in its effect.

speak.title: Role-play: which bottle should we buy?
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: You are in a shop with a friend. You want to buy the bottle with green leaves and the word eco on it. Explain why you like it and why you think it is a good choice.

b.text: You are not sure the label is true. Ask what the label really proves. Ask at least two questions, then decide together which bottle to buy.

phrases: I'd like to buy this one, it looks greener.
What's the label actually telling us?
I'm not sure we can trust it.
Let's check the figures before we decide.
Shall we buy the plain one instead?
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class which bottle you chose and why.
